Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 70
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Fashion Designer
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Media / News: Related news, Loss of Control: Lack of control
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost, Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me, Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe
  Memory: Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Vignette:
Elena is seventy years old, and for the first time in her life, her design studio feels like a hostile space. The cool marble of the cutting table, once a smooth and reassuring surface under her hands, now feels predatory. It has been eight months since she lost her granddaughter, Sofia, and the world has rearranged itself into a landscape of threats. The change began on a Tuesday afternoon in a small downtown bistro, a place Elena had chosen for its bright, airy atmosphere. She and Sofia were celebrating Sofia’s acceptance into art school. The memory, when it comes, is never a choice; it forces its way in, a brutal takeover of the present. One moment she is unspooling a bolt of silk, the next she is back on the bistro’s cold tile floor, the shock of the temperature radiating through her knees. It is not a thought but a full-body re-enactment: the scent of espresso and bleach, the shattering glass, the single, deafening crack that followed, and the sight of Sofia crumpling to the ground. In these moments, which can be triggered by something as simple as a news van siren on the street below her window, it feels so completely real that she sometimes reaches out a hand to stop a fall that happened months ago.

In the weeks that followed the shooting, a deep and unshakeable conviction settled within her. She was certain that the event happened because of her actions. If she hadn't insisted on that particular bistro, if she had just screamed a second sooner, if she hadn't frozen when the man with the frantic eyes burst through the door, she could have protected Sofia. This thought loops endlessly, a prosecutor in her own mind. The fact that the man was never caught, that he faced no consequences for what he did, has curdled into a constant, low-grade sense of injustice and fear. The world is not safe because he is still in it, and she failed in her most essential duty to keep her family safe within it. This belief has become the architect of her new life.

Her husband, Marco, tries to bring the world back to her, but she cannot let it in. He will turn on the evening news, and the familiar cadence of the anchor’s voice is enough to send a jolt of panic through her. She will leave the room, unable to bear the risk of hearing another story of random violence, which she is sure would confirm her belief that the world is fundamentally dangerous and that she is powerless within it. Her avoidance has become a full-time job. She has meticulously dismantled the shrine of Sofia’s pictures in their living room, packing away the smiling photos because each one is a reminder of her failure. This has created a silent, painful rift with her son, who feels she is trying to erase his daughter. Even moments of happiness feel treacherous. Last month, on their anniversary, Marco brought her a new set of charcoals for sketching. For a fleeting second, she felt a spark of the old creative joy, but it was immediately extinguished by a wave of guilt. She had come to believe that feeling good was a betrayal of Sofia’s memory, an unforgivable indulgence when her granddaughter could no longer feel anything at all. She pushes these positive emotions away, finding a strange safety in the persistent grayness of her grief.

Her work, once her passion, now offers no refuge. The textures, colors, and designs that used to bring her life feel meaningless. Her hands, which could once coax a perfect garment from a flat piece of cloth, now tremble. The business is faltering, but the financial toll is secondary to the loss of self. She sought help after a particularly vivid flashback in her studio, triggered by the cool air from a vent blowing on her skin. She found herself on the floor, weeping, surrounded by half-finished designs that felt like relics from another person’s life. What frightened her most was not the memory itself, but the growing sense that the vibrant, creative woman she once was had died in that bistro alongside her granddaughter, and she has no idea how to bring her back.
